extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator: educated eighteenth-century public — theatre-goers, literary readers, and schoolmasters/parents
extracted.subtask_description: A series of Spectator essays giving prescriptive advice on theatrical taste (tone, epilogues, music), principles of poetic sublimity, and concrete methods for moral education in schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain tonal unity between tragedy and its close
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not tack a comic epilogue onto a tragic play because it extinguishes the audience's emotion and makes noble achievements seem silly. The essay objects to the 'most unnatural Tack of the Comick Tail to the Tragick Head.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the author felt the merry epilogue after Andromache destroyed the melancholy the tragedy had produced; anti-patterns include concluding a solemn performance with a comic piece that 'jumbles' the audience's soul. Suggested practice: preserve the emotional unity of a tragic performance; if refreshment is required, choose forms that do not undercut the tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve audience emotional continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience's heightened feeling at the end of a tragedy should not be dissipated by subsequent frivolity; some patrons even leave before epilogues to keep the melancholic impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behavioural advice for theatre-goers: if you value the preservation of the play's effect, depart before a comick epilogue; as a critic, assess a production by whether the close leaves the audience 'all of a Piece' or 'jumbled' between Jest and Earnest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suit music to place and business
rubrics_metrics.description: Musicians (e.g., church organists) must adapt their airs to the context: the musician is obliged to 'keep to the Text as much as the Preacher.' Music foreign to the service (merry jigs) is prejudicial to pious audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example/anti-pattern: church organists imitating theaterly epilogues in farewell voluntaries; recommended: match musical style to liturgical purpose and avoid incongruous levity that dissipates devotional feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach virtue alongside letters in schools
rubrics_metrics.description: Masters should care as much for 'fashioning the Manners of their Scholars' as for forming their tongues to Greek and Latin; virtue ought to be taught and strengthened concurrently with learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General prescription: make moral instruction a central, deliberate part of schooling rather than subordinating it to linguistic training. The essay cites Locke and argues moral formation is more important than mere classical proficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require pupils to state and justify opinions on readings
rubrics_metrics.description: When students read the lives and actions of famous men, they should not merely parse sentences but be asked their opinion of actions and obliged to give reasons why they judge them good or bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogical exercise: task pupils to analyze actions (e.g., Turnus and Aeneas), to censure or approve particulars, and to show how actions might be improved — this strengthens judgment on courage, temperance, honour, and justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach balanced appraisal of exemplars (avoid idolizing characters in gross)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not recommend an example 'in gross'; instead teach wherein a great man had weaknesses as well as strengths so that pupils do not confound beauties with blemishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Alexander's cruelty explained via formative influence (Lysimachus); method prevents blind admiration and helps pupils distinguish admirable features from faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contemporary exemplars and misfortunes to dissuade vice (Horace's method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Displaying the miserable condition or shameful actions of contemporaries teaches youth to avoid luxury, debauchery, and other vices; Horace's father's practice of citing real examples is recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogical technique: point to the fate of specific contemporaries (e.g., Burr, Son of Albus, Trebonius) to instil aversion to particular vices; analogy: patients heed physicians when they hear of neighbouring deaths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice judgment by mutual accusation and arbitration (Xenophon model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt exercises where pupils hear mutual accusations (violence, cheating, slander, ingratitude) and learn to give judgments, thereby training principles of justice and sobriety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classroom practice: governors hear disputes and require pupils to adjudicate; builds real judicial reasoning and moral discernment (Xenophon's Schools of Equity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Require daily accountability for use of time (Indian Gymnosophists model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before meals, masters should ask each scholar how he spent the morning; any who cannot account for productive use of time are excluded from dinner and obliged to work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary method: daily reporting fosters diligence; anti-pattern: tolerating idle scholars who cannot justify their time-use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinforce practical charity and prudence via small provisos (sixpence exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasionally give each scholar a small sum (sixpence) to spend, require next-day account; a fixed portion (one third) must be for charity and pupils are commended or blamed on their choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete exercise to teach generosity, prudence, and reporting; use small stakes to create habitual moral decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate celebrated authors when writing in a sublime mode
rubrics_metrics.description: To succeed in the sublime, a writer should imitate celebrated predecessors who wrote on the same subject (e.g., consider how Homer would have spoken on a poetical occasion); imitation can light the flame without servility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stylistic prescription: study masters in the same genre, absorb their spirit while avoiding slavish copying; example: many passages in Virgil were 'lighted up by Homer,' and Milton used imitation effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish sublimity from passionate pathos (Longinus's point)
rubrics_metrics.description: Loftiness in sentiments can exist without passion; the pathetic may animate the sublime but is not essential to it — a composed majesty can produce sublime effects without tumult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary criterion: evaluate sublime writing by grandeur of ideas and composed majesty, not merely by how it stirs passion; example: Milton's Book 7 as 'the Ocean in a Calm' producing sublime impressions without agitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use authoritative/allusive sources judiciously to enrich poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate allusions (e.g., Scripture) raise poetic grandeur where suited; Milton wisely uses scriptural hints and high strains fitted to his readers' imaginations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating subjects (like Creation), draw on high authorities (Scripture, prophetic imagery) where relevant, and qualify such strains to the reader's imaginative pitch; examples include the Messiah and chariots imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question clarity vs poetic density in dramatic dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Raises the question whether characters in tragedy should 'always talk to be understood' — a tension between natural comprehensibility and higher poetic/dramatic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical diagnostic: consider whether dialogue's obscurities are a defect or intentional artistic elevation; assess plays both by natural immediate understanding (as the Knight claims to 'know the Meaning of' every sentence) and by adherence to dramatic rules.
